passage:
Internship supervisor's note, week six. Kavitha, analytics team.
Shalini is a careful intern, and her numbers are always right. But she still builds every report by hand in the old spreadsheet, copying data from four files, which takes most of her Thursday. The team moved to the shared dashboard tool a month ago; I showed her once, and she said it looked good. When I asked why she hadn't switched, she smiled. "I'm happy with my way. It works." Then, more quietly: "Learning the new one would take a whole day." She stays late every Thursday.
What I did: I blocked two hours on Monday for us to rebuild one report together in the new tool.

qa.q: How many files does Shalini copy data from?
qa.a: Shalini copies data from four files.

qa.q: What does Shalini's quieter remark about learning the new tool reveal?
qa.a: It reveals that "I'm happy with my way" is partly about avoiding the effort of change; the inertia feels like contentment to her.

qa.q: Why is rebuilding one report together a good step?
qa.a: It makes the switch small and supported, so Shalini can see the time saved without having to find a whole free day alone.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see Shalini's work habits?
qa.a: Kavitha values Shalini's careful, correct numbers but can see the late Thursdays and wants to help her move to a better tool.

grounding: Shows a young adult staying with a slow old method only because switching takes effort, calling it being happy with it.

passage:
Sunday night
Sudha showed me today that she pays half what I do for the same mobile data. Half! My plan is the one Papa set up when I was in Class 9, and I've just... kept it. She sent me the link to switch; it takes about fifteen minutes and a visit to the shop for a new SIM. I said, "Nah, mine's fine, I'm used to it." And I am fine, honestly. It works. But I did the maths on the bus: over a year, the difference would pay for the headphones I keep saying I can't afford. So why haven't I clicked? It's not that I love my plan. I just don't want to do the thing.
Tanvir

qa.q: How long does switching take, according to the link?
qa.a: It takes about fifteen minutes and a visit to the shop for a new SIM.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir say "mine's fine, I'm used to it"?
qa.a: Staying needs no effort, so the old plan feels like a comfortable choice; but Tanvir admits it isn't love for the plan, just not wanting to do the switch.

qa.q: What small step could Tanvir take this week?
qa.a: Tanvir could set aside fifteen minutes to click the link and visit the shop, perhaps with Sudha, so the change feels like one small task.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel when Tanvir says "Nah"?
qa.a: Sudha may feel amused or puzzled, having found an easy saving and watched a friend shrug it off.

grounding: Shows a young adult staying on an overpriced plan only because changing needs effort, and calling the inertia being fine.

passage: For two years, Ankita had taken the private bus from her town near Karnal to college: forty rupees each way, packed, forty-five minutes of loud film songs. In January a new state bus started on the same route, twenty rupees, half-empty, twenty-five minutes. Her friend Jyoti switched on day one. "Come with me tomorrow," Jyoti said. "No, I'm fine. I know the private bus conductor, I know where to stand. It's comfortable." But Ankita still arrived late and tired every day, and she'd told Jyoti twice that month she was short of money for photocopies. "Comfortable?" Jyoti said. "You complain every day." Ankita laughed. "I'm just used to it." She thought about it that night. Changing meant a new stop, a new timetable, a new conductor. That was all. The next morning she waited at the state bus stop, a little nervous, with Jyoti.

qa.q: How much did the new state bus cost?
qa.a: Twenty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Ankita say she was "fine" on the private bus?
qa.a: It was familiar, and changing felt like effort, a new stop and timetable, so she called her habit comfortable even though she complained daily.

qa.q: What helped Ankita finally switch buses?
qa.a: Thinking it through that night and seeing that changing only meant a new stop, timetable and conductor. Going with Jyoti made the first morning easier.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel waiting at the state bus stop with Ankita?
qa.a: Jyoti is probably pleased and a bit amused, having watched Ankita complain for weeks while calling it comfortable.

grounding: A young woman keeps taking a slower, costlier bus only because it's familiar, calling it comfortable, until she sees how small the change is.

passage: In Edinburgh, Freya had been paying for a meal-kit subscription since her first term. Every week a box arrived: three recipes, measured spices, a little card. She didn't much like the food, and it cost almost twice what she'd spend at the market. Alejandro, her flatmate, watched her leave half a box of vegetables to wilt again. "Why don't you cancel it?" "It's fine. It's easy," she said. "Is it? You never cook two of the three." Freya shrugged. "Cancelling means logging in, finding the page, answering their 'are you sure' questions. And then I'd have to plan meals." "So you're paying extra to avoid ten minutes." She opened her mouth to argue, then closed it. That evening she found the cancel page. It took seven minutes. On Saturday she and Alejandro walked to the market together, and she bought just what she wanted.

qa.q: How long did it take Freya to cancel the subscription?
qa.a: It took seven minutes.

qa.q: Why did Freya say the subscription was "fine" even though she didn't like it?
qa.a: Cancelling and planning meals felt like effort, so staying felt easier. She called it fine because change seemed like work, not because she was really happy.

qa.q: What turned Freya's thinking around, and what did she do next?
qa.a: Alejandro saying she was paying extra to avoid ten minutes. She found the cancel page that evening and went to the market on Saturday.

qa.q: How might Alejandro feel walking to the market with Freya?
qa.a: Alejandro might feel glad she made the change, and perhaps relieved to stop watching vegetables wilt in their shared fridge. 🙂

grounding: A young woman abroad keeps an overpriced meal-kit subscription only because cancelling feels like effort, until her flatmate points it out.

passage:
Academic adviser's note, second-year advising, 12 August
Ishita came for her elective sign-off. For the third semester in a row she has chosen the basic spreadsheet course, now at level 2, taught from the same slides. When I asked why, she said, "It's fine, I'm used to it." Her friend Jasleen, who took the data design elective, had told her it was hard but "finally interesting." Ishita admitted she had read that syllabus and liked it, but switching meant a new timetable, new classmates and a waitlist form. "Honestly, I'm content where I am," she said, looking at the floor. I showed her the waitlist form: one page, due Friday. She took it with her. I will check with her on Friday.

qa.q: Which elective did Jasleen take?
qa.a: The data design elective.

qa.q: What does Ishita looking at the floor suggest about her content answer?
qa.a: It suggests she may feel less content than she says, perhaps bored or uneasy, and is staying mainly because switching feels like effort.

qa.q: What did the adviser make easier, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Showing her the one-page waitlist form due Friday, which makes switching less effort so a real choice becomes possible.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel if Ishita joins the data design elective?
qa.a: Jasleen would probably feel glad to have her friend in a class she finds finally interesting.

grounding: An adviser records a student staying in a weak course because switching takes effort, while calling it contentment.

passage:
Sunday night
Realised today I've studied in bed every night for two years, laptop on my knees, and I fall asleep by page three every single time. Hafsa goes to the reading room on the second floor at seven. She finishes in two hours what takes me four.
She asked me again tonight, "Come with me?" I said, "Nah, I'm comfortable here." And I am comfortable. That's the problem. It's not that I love the bed. It's that going means shoes, a bag, a walk, finding a seat. Changing feels like a whole project, so I tell myself I'm happy.
Tomorrow: shoes by the door at 6:45. Just one night. If it's awful, fine.
Jaya

qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: What is Jaya feeling about the bed habit?
qa.a: Jaya feels comfortable but uneasy, noticing that the comfort is really a way of dodging the small effort of change.

qa.q: Why is shoes by the door at 6:45, just one night, a good plan?
qa.a: It makes the change tiny and easy to start, so effort no longer hides behind feeling content.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel if Jaya finally comes along?
qa.a: Hafsa would probably feel pleased, since she keeps inviting Jaya to the reading room.

grounding: A student's diary shows a weak study habit kept only because changing takes effort, dressed up as being comfortable.

passage: In Seoul, Mina studied every afternoon at the same noisy café near her university. She'd gone there since first year. The music was loud, the chairs uncomfortable, and she often read one page three times. Her friend Oskar, an exchange student, found a quiet library room with good lamps and big desks. "Come with me. I finish twice as much." Mina smiled. "I'm used to my café. It's fine." But her exam results were slipping. She told herself she liked the atmosphere. passage: In the university hostel in Aligarh, Yusuf had eaten at Mess A for three years. The food was often cold and repetitive. Mess B, across the lawn, had better food and cost the same; his friend Vishal had switched in second year. "Come to B," Vishal kept saying. "The dal is actually good." Yusuf always said, "I'm fine here. I'm used to it." Switching meant filling a form at the warden's office, getting a new card, sitting with new people. It felt like effort. One evening, Mess A served the same watery dal for the fourth time that week. Yusuf pushed it around the plate and told himself he wasn't that hungry. Across the lawn, laughter came from Mess B. He thought, maybe next semester, and felt an odd heaviness he called being settled.

qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: Why does Yusuf keep eating at Mess A despite the food?
qa.a: Switching means a form, a new card and new people, so staying feels easier, and he tells himself he's settled even though he feels an odd heaviness.

qa.q: What could Yusuf do to test the switch?

passage:
Dear Madhuri,

Guess what I finally did today? I switched my phone plan.

I know, very exciting. But listen. I had been on the same plan since Class 11. It cost more than double what the new ones cost, and gave half the data. Every month I'd see the bill and think, I should change. Then I'd think about calling customer care, the forms, the new SIM, and I'd just... not.

I told myself I was fine with it. "It works, why change?" But I wasn't fine. I just didn't want the effort.

This morning I timed it. The switch took twenty-two minutes.

Four years. Twenty-two minutes.

I'm now looking at everything else I've been "fine" with. My gym I never go to. The coaching I don't like. Maybe some of those are just inertia too.

Love,
Himani

qa.q: How long did the switch take?
qa.a: The switch took twenty-two minutes.

qa.q: Why did Himani stay on the old plan for so long?
qa.a: Himani felt the effort of switching was too much, and kept saying it was fine, so inertia felt like contentment.

qa.q: What could Himani do about the other things called "fine"?
qa.a: Himani could check each one, like the gym and coaching, and ask whether staying is a choice or just to avoid effort.

qa.q: How might Madhuri react to this letter?
qa.a: Madhuri might feel amused by the twenty-two minutes and encouraged to check Madhuri's own habits.

grounding: A young adult realises the overpriced phone plan lasted for years only because switching needed effort.

passage:
You want to know why I wasted a whole semester, Ujjwal? Okay. I'm Vidya, and it's a bit embarrassing.

In second year, I enrolled in a data analysis elective. By week three I knew it was badly taught. The lecturer read slides aloud. I learned more from free videos.

There was a much better elective, design thinking, with a great teacher. Switching was allowed until week five. All I had to do was fill one form and talk to the coordinator.

I kept meaning to. Every week, I'd think, next week. I told my friends, "It's fine, it's not that bad." And I honestly thought I was content.

Week five came and went. I stayed.

At the end of the semester, my friend who'd switched showed me her project. It was brilliant. I felt this sick drop in my stomach.

I wasn't content. I was just stuck. And I'd called it contentment so I wouldn't have to move.

qa.q: Until which week was switching allowed?
qa.a: Switching was allowed until week five.

qa.q: Why did Vidya stay in the weak elective?
qa.a: Vidya didn't want the small effort of switching and told herself it was fine, so inertia felt like contentment.

qa.q: What could Vidya do next time she notices a better option?
qa.a: Vidya could act on it straight away, like filling the form that day, instead of waiting for next week.

qa.q: How might Vidya's friend have felt showing her project?
qa.a: The friend probably felt proud and excited about the project, perhaps not realising how it made Vidya feel.

grounding: A young adult stays in a weak elective only because switching needs effort, and later sees the inertia was not contentment.

passage:
First week of July. Chinmay's PG was forty minutes from college by two buses. His friend Hrithik mentioned a new PG opening right next to campus, cheaper, with better food. "Come see it." Chinmay said, "Mine's fine."

Late August. Chinmay missed two morning lectures because of bus delays in the rain. He told Hrithik, "It's okay, I'm used to it." But he was tired every evening. The new PG still had a room free.

Early October. Hrithik sat on Chinmay's bed. "Why haven't you moved? It's closer, cheaper, better."

Chinmay opened his mouth to say "Mine's fine" again. Then he stopped. "Because moving is a whole thing. Packing, telling the owner, finding a van."

"So you're not happy here. You just don't want to move."

Chinmay looked around the cramped room. "I've been calling it fine because changing felt like work."

He went to see the new PG that evening.

qa.q: How far was Chinmay's PG from college?
qa.a: Forty minutes from college by two buses.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay keep saying his PG was fine?
qa.a: Chinmay felt that moving would be a hassle, so he told himself he was content even though he was tired and missing lectures.

qa.q: What did Hrithik say that helped Chinmay see the problem?
qa.a: Hrithik pointed out that Chinmay wasn't happy, just avoiding the effort of moving, which helped him see the inertia.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel when Chinmay finally went to see the new PG?
qa.a: Hrithik probably felt relieved and pleased, having suggested it three months earlier.

grounding: Over three months, a young adult stays in a distant PG only because moving needs effort, calling it being fine.
